newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ICRC head leads tribute to staff slain in Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: ICRC head leads tribute to staff slain in Chechnya.

text.p: The head of the International Committee of the Red Cross led 500 mourners on Friday in praising six ICRC staff slain in Chechnya for their "solidarity with the victims" of the conflict in the breakaway region.

It was the third time in four years that Cornelio Sommaruga, president of the Swiss-run ICRC, has delivered a eulogy at a memorial service at Geneva's Saint Peter's Cathedral for agency staff brutally killed in the field.
"We are in mourning, horrified by this revolting massacre. It is the profound mourning of everyone in the humanitarian world and their friends," Sommaruga said.

"The ICRC is profundly shocked and grieved by this tragedy and cannot but vigorously condemn this attack on the very core of what the Red Cross originally was set out to do and still is: the medical mission to prevent and alleviate human suffering."

The five women medical workers and male construction manager -- from Canada, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway and Spain -- follow three Swiss staff killed in an ambush in Burundi last June and a Swiss slain on a convoy entering Sarajevo in 1992.
The bodies of the latest victims, shot in their beds on Tuesday at a Red Cross hospital compound southwest of Grozny, were brought to Geneva on Wednesday and have been flown home since.

Sommaruga, flanked by Vladimir Petrovsky, director general of the U.N. European headquarters in Geneva, later took part in a silent march organised by the staff associations of the two organisations. Nearly 1,000 humanitarian workers attended.

Sommaruga, recalling the deceased in front of a crowd of ICRC staff and Geneva dignitaries gathered at the Protestant Cathedral where Jean Calvin preached, said: "You were engaged in one of the most difficult and dangerous ICRC missions.

"The attitude of the authorities and of the local population after the tragedy has shown well the unique value of your work. Thousands of victims whom you cared for and whose lives you saved mourn at your death," he added.

As the ceremony was held in Geneva, Itar-Tass news agency reported the security service of Chechnya's separatist government saying it had detained several people suspected of involvement in the murders at Novye Atagi.

Security service head Abu Movsayev told Tass he could not disclose the names or nationalities of those held. He said his agency had every reason for believing that the killings were politically motivated.

ICRC said that it would issue a round-up of testimony later in the day from 14 ICRC staff who survived the attack by unknown masked gunmen. Some told reporters at Geneva airport that they -- unlike the victims -- had locked their doors at bedtime.
"All six were dedicated to the ideal of solidarity with the victims of the Chechen conflict," said Sommaruga, a former Swiss diplomat who has headed the Geneva-based agency since 1988.
"They were fulfilling with exemplary enthusiasm the original mission of the Red Cross -- to care for wounded," he added.
Sommaruga described the humanitarian career of each, noting Gunnhild Myklebust, 55, one of two slain Norwegian Red Cross nurses, had become a grandmother while serving in Chechnya.
Fernanda Calado, 49-year-old chief nurse from Spain, had worked for ICRC for 12 years in conflict zones including Angola, Israel, Cambodia, Somalia, and Rwanda.
"Every one of us feels deep in his or her heart the dreadful blow dealt so brutally to the victims' families on the eve of the festive season," the ICRC president added.

The victims were: Hans Elkerbout (47, construction technician, Netherlands Red Cross), Ingeborg Foss (42, nurse, Norwegian Red Cross), Nancy Malloy (51, medical administrator, Canadian Red Cross), Gunnhild Myklebust (55, nurse, Norwegian Red Cross) and Sheryl Thayer (40, nurse, New Zealand Red Cross) and Fernanda Calado, 49, a Spanish nurse under contract to ICRC.
